# Lightning session G: Internationalisation

Day 2, 14:30 · Alizée Baudez, a second community speaker · lightning · coverage: transcript

Alizée Baudez (International SEO Consultant) on language, region and authority, named from her self-introduction, which matches the official speaker list; then Zahra Laleh's talk on non-Latin scripts, presented on her behalf by a colleague who was not named; a second attendee recording covers the rest of that talk.

## Claims

- **[Stage]** In a community speaker's audit case, a premium multifunctional-furniture maker about to be acquired had multilingual sites with clean translations by native speakers and hreflang tags that were in fairly good shape.
  <br><sub>`D2-C618` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** In the same furniture-maker audit, the Dutch site had only a fraction of the conversions of the brand's other language sites, although it showed the same catalogue, the same hero products and the same photography.
  <br><sub>`D2-C619` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Checking a competitor during the furniture-maker audit, a community speaker found that a large furniture retailer's French and Dutch sites differ a little in the products they show and especially in their photography, with items apparently shown in much smaller rooms on the Dutch site.
  <br><sub>`D2-C620` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said her first guess, that Dutch homes are smaller than French ones, was wrong: Dutch and French homes have about the same floor area per person, and what differs is the type of house.
  <br><sub>`D2-C621` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said about 19% of homes in Europe are terraced houses on several floors, against 58% in the Netherlands; the matching Eurostat figures are 2019 shares of the EU and Dutch population living in semi-detached or terraced houses, not shares of homes.
  <br><sub>`D2-C622` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** In a community speaker's comparison, a typical Dutch home is narrow and spread over several levels, often with very steep, narrow staircases that make furniture harder to install upstairs, while a typical French home has a wide ground floor and usually wide stairs.
  <br><sub>`D2-C623` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The lesson of the furniture-maker case was that the translation was correct but the target region had never been checked.
  > "the translation was right, but the region was never checked"
  <br><sub>`D2-C624` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** When translations and hreflang are clean but one country version converts far worse, compare that market's product range, photography and delivery or installation constraints with local competitors before changing anything technical.
  <br><sub>`D2-C625` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker framed international SEO around three signals to settle before working on hreflang: language (what people can read), region (who the content is for) and authority (why local people should trust the site).
  <br><sub>`D2-C626` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said language versions need adjusting for regional variants of one language: 90 is 'quatre-vingt-dix' in France but 'nonante' in Belgium, and Swiss German differs from German, for example in whether the letter ß (Eszett) is used.
  <br><sub>`D2-C627` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez) · Extends [D2-C562](D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's documentation recommends hreflang annotations even when a site's versions differ only by small regional variations within one language, for example English-language content targeted to the US, GB and Ireland.
  <br><sub>`D2-C628` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · is the documentation · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Settling the region means deciding who the content is actually for, which shapes how the catalogue is organised, how prices look and which payment options each market gets.
  <br><sub>`D2-C629` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Of language, region and authority, a community speaker called language easy to settle and region solvable with a little research, while authority (why local people should trust a brand) has to be earned and built over time.
  <br><sub>`D2-C630` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker stressed that an hreflang annotation for a country (her example was German for Austria, de-AT) does not by itself make a site established or trusted in that country; local authority has to be worked for.
  <br><sub>`D2-C631` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez) · consistent with Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions), [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's documentation lists the signals it uses to decide which locale a page targets: ccTLDs, hreflang statements, server location, and other signals such as local addresses and phone numbers, local language and currency, links from other local sites and Business Profile signals.
  <br><sub>`D2-C632` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · is the documentation · [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites) · Used by `DEV-INT-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker cited a Semrush study that found at least one hreflang error on 75% of multilingual websites; the study, reported in February 2017, audited 20,000 sites with several language versions (the speaker recalled it as about five years old).
  <br><sub>`D2-C633` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez) · not in Google docs · [75% of Multilingual Websites Have Hreflang Implementation Mistakes](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/75-multilingual-websites-hreflang-implementation-mistakes/185737/)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said the SEO industry has treated hreflang as the hard part of international SEO; hreflang is complicated, but the real hard part is the homework of understanding consumers in each market.
  > "the hard part is actually doing the homework to understand your consumers"
  <br><sub>`D2-C634` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said the answers about what consumers in each market want expire, because regional differences change over time.
  <br><sub>`D2-C635` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker showed a chart of search interest over time for ceiling fans in northern versus southern Europe, saying southern Europeans commonly have them at home while northern Europeans paid them no attention until the previous summer's heat waves (the talk was on 1 October 2026).
  <br><sub>`D2-C636` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Re-check regional demand for core product categories at least once a year, for example by comparing regions and seasons in Google Trends, because climate, housing or habits can shift what a market wants.
  <br><sub>`D2-C637` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Stage]** The first of three questions to ask before the technical work of international SEO is which languages, and which language variants, the site actually serves, keeping languages and variants apart.
  <br><sub>`D2-C638` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The second question before international SEO work is what genuinely differs between the regions of each language, such as photography, content, vocabulary, the way products are presented, pricing, catalogues and payment options.
  <br><sub>`D2-C639` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The third question is whether you can name three local sources that already treat the brand as present in a country; if you cannot, a community speaker advised not to expand there but to fix the markets you already serve.
  > "don't bother expanding to another country; just fix the ones you already have"
  <br><sub>`D2-C640` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Treat hreflang as a way to show the right language version, not as a market-entry signal: before launching a country version, make sure local publications, partners or directories already mention the brand, and localise pricing and payment options.
  <br><sub>`D2-C641` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Analysis]** List language variants such as fr-FR and fr-BE or de-DE and de-CH separately in a site's language inventory, and give each its own vocabulary and spelling review instead of reusing one translation for every country.
  <br><sub>`D2-C642` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community talk, presented on its author's behalf by a colleague, was about multilingual SEO for languages written in non-Latin scripts, such as Persian and Arabic.
  <br><sub>`D2-C643` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Arabic and Persian contain letters that look identical to users but are different characters to software, with different Unicode code points; the example given was the letter ye, which has an Arabic and a Persian form.
  <br><sub>`D2-C644` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Because Arabic and Persian lookalike letters have different code points, a searcher may type one variant of a word while a website's text uses the other.
  <br><sub>`D2-C645` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Lookalike Arabic and Persian character variants cause problems for data analysis and keyword research: data for one term can be split across the variants, which makes keyword research less accurate.
  <br><sub>`D2-C646` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For Persian and Arabic keyword research, look up each lookalike-character spelling of a term separately and add up the volumes, and check which variant the site's own content uses.
  <br><sub>`D2-C647` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Stage]** Persian and Arabic are written right to left and English left to right, so a title that mixes the two scripts can display in a confusing, unpredictable order even when its content is correct.
  <br><sub>`D2-C963` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-INT-12`, the glossary term *Bidirectional text*</sub>

- **[Stage]** The display problem of mixing right-to-left and left-to-right text also affects product titles and URLs, the presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said, showing an example from a large Iranian e-commerce site.
  <br><sub>`D2-C964` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-INT-12`, the glossary term *Bidirectional text*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Users of non-Latin-script languages do not always search in their own script: the same Persian query may be typed in Persian script or in Latin letters, with the same intent and the same expected results.
  <br><sub>`D2-C965` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · consistent with Google docs · [How Google Search handles multilingual searches](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/09/multilingual-searches) · Extends [D2-C599](D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) · Used by `DEV-INT-11`, the glossary term *Transliterated queries*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Keyword research for non-Latin-script languages should ask how people actually type and spell in local search, not only what the right keyword is, because switching keyboards is inconvenient, especially when typing on mobile.
  <br><sub>`D2-C966` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said that in competitive Persian, Turkish and Arabic searches, bought backlinks and paid editorial content still visibly influence rankings and are widespread (an observation; no data was shown); the presenter stressed this described the situation and was not a recommendation.
  <br><sub>`D2-C967` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** The presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said Google announced in October 2023 that it had improved its spam-detection coverage for languages: the spam policy was global, but the coverage improvement was language-specific.
  <br><sub>`D2-C968` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · confirmed by Google docs · [October 2023 Spam Update](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/10/october-2023-spam-update)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said Persian offers far fewer natural link opportunities than English, with fewer publications, niche blogs and websites.
  <br><sub>`D2-C969` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For SEO in languages such as Persian, the presenter of the non-Latin-script talk advised accepting different competitive dynamics and basing strategy on the actual maturity of that language's market, not only on the global policy.
  <br><sub>`D2-C970` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google search features often launch in some languages or countries first and expand later (the presenter's example was site names, launched in several languages and then extended to all languages in 2023), so comparisons of performance across languages and countries should not assume a feature is live everywhere at once.
  <br><sub>`D2-C971` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · confirmed by Google docs · [Site names on Google Search now available for all languages](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/09/site-names-global-rollout)</sub>

- **[Stage]** In the presenter's observation, AI answers to Persian queries are written in Persian but cite some English sources; the presenter explained that Persian content on a topic is often thinner, of lower quality or less relevant, so the systems retrieve from languages with better content, which the presenter called cross-lingual retrieval.
  <br><sub>`D2-C972` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · consistent with Google docs · [Translated results in Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/translated-results), [How Google Search handles multilingual searches](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/09/multilingual-searches) · Extends [D2-C603](D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The non-Latin-script talk concluded that multilingual SEO is not just translation: script, language behaviour and market maturity also matter, and basic SEO tactics, though the same everywhere, must be fitted to each market.
  <br><sub>`D2-C973` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The presenter of the non-Latin-script talk recalled that Google officially treats buying links for ranking as spam (the year of the announcement was not clear in the recording).
  <br><sub>`D2-C977` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · confirmed by Google docs · [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's October 2023 spam update post (4 October 2023) says the update improved coverage in many languages and spam types, cleaning up spam reported in Turkish, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Hindi, Chinese and other languages, particularly cloaking, hacked, auto-generated and scraped spam.
  <br><sub>`D2-C978` · Search Central blog (4 October 2023) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · is the documentation · [October 2023 Spam Update](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/10/october-2023-spam-update)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The October 2023 spam update cited in the non-Latin-script talk names neither Persian nor Arabic (only 'other languages') and lists cloaking, hacked, auto-generated and scraped spam, not link spam, so it does not show that the bought links the presenter saw working in Persian or Arabic search were addressed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C979` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · [October 2023 Spam Update](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/10/october-2023-spam-update), [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's site names were introduced on mobile results for select languages in October 2022, expanded to desktop in March 2023, and on 7 September 2023 became available in all languages where Google Search is available, on mobile and desktop.
  <br><sub>`D2-C980` · Search Central blog (7 September 2023) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · is the documentation · [Site names on Google Search now available for all languages](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/09/site-names-global-rollout)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's post on multilingual searches (8 September 2023) says that, because of typing difficulty on some keyboards, a person in India might search in Hindi using Latin rather than Devanagari characters and want and receive Hindi results written either way.
  <br><sub>`D2-C981` · Search Central blog (8 September 2023) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation · is the documentation · [How Google Search handles multilingual searches](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/09/multilingual-searches) · Used by `DEV-INT-11`, the glossary term *Transliterated queries*</sub>
